b: I just watched the NestWorks C500 official unboxing video (linked at the end of the post).
It sounds a bit bizarre, but that immediately sent my thoughts towards “I WANT ONE.”
I have been shopping for a benchtop CNC for a very long time.

I have a Carbide 3D Nomad that I haven’t enjoyed using. Part of that’s on me. I have a benchtop mill that I am ready to convert to CNC as soon as I can spare the time. It’s been years, and will probably take a while longer.
Makera sent over a Z1 for testing. It’s very capable for its class. I think it’s maybe 90% of the way towards a recommendable beginner solution.

I want a more capable machine with quality of life features, such as an automatic tool changer and automatic lubrication system. A high-power spindle and as much rigidity as can be mustered in a benchtop package.
There’s the Langmuir MR-1 (see The Langmuir MR-1 is a Different Kind of CNC Mill), but I don’t want another kit, and especially not one filled with concrete that I couldn’t move down the road.
There are parts I want to make, and I want it done easily and quickly. Yes, I know that’s not how it works. CNC milling is not as quick as importing a file into a slicer and hitting “print.”
But there are lots of chores that you need to deal with at the hobbyist-level size and budget. Until now. Or at least that’s what I’m hoping.
The NestWorks C500 is very expensive with a $6499 preorder price. Plus you need a stand. And accessories. Oh, so many accessories and tooling.
Maybe the price will relax by the time I can budget for one. And by then early adopters will have identified any issues that Nestworks will have already fixed.
On paper, it’s a larger benchtop machine with appealing big-machine features.
But what I really liked about the Nestworks C500 unboxing video was the step by step approach.
They hold your hand, but in a way that comes across well.
In one part, they advise the user to grab the thoughtfully-placed hex key, use the short end to loosen the hold-down fasteners, and then the long end to remove the fasteners the rest of the way.

That’s “hex keys 101” knowledge right there. Did they have to mention it in the video? But for those who haven’t used hex keys before, that’s good info. For the “duh, that’s obvious” folks, the beginner knowledge doesn’t get in the way. Or at least I didn’t mind it.
It looks like the Nestworks team put conscious effort towards making the C500 a more advanced machine that is still beginner-friendly.
What I really hope is that they do the same and put the same care towards their software, learning guides, and things like maintenance tasks.
“One click toolpath generation.” I sure hope Nestworks isn’t exaggerating with their CAM and other software claims.
CNC is complex. You’ve cut a round contour into the top of your part. Great, you now have to flip it and carve a different shape into the bottom. How do you hold the part securely?

“Use double-sided tape” can only get you so far and only with certain materials. The same with hold-downs. Vacuum tables, vise jaws, tool pallets – there are loads of work-holding methods that require some guidance to use and use effectively.
Nestworks’ unboxing video gave me a glimmer of hope that we’ll see a lot more hand-holding.
I’m really hoping that this opens up the category between benchtop toys and “it’d better make you money” options such as from Tormach.
And I know it sounds strange that something like an unboxing video can generate so much optimism in me. It’s that, plus what I saw from all the Kickstarter videos.

All of that is also compounded with my very long search for a capable machine that checks all my boxes. I want a machine that can create complex parts while requiring less of my presence than if I were to do the work by hand.
At the least, brands like Nestworks are creating more competition, and that will drive innovation. Hopefully.

Personally, while I might eventually be able to justify the price, I think Nestworks would be smart to also launch machines in the $2500 price range, which is what plenty of folks are spending on flagship 3D printers.

There’s also a chance that more capable machines of this size will attract interest from small production houses and 3D print farms. 3D printing companies have been buying up consumer-grade machines from companies like Bambu, and I’m sure that this sales volume has helped drive things forward. If the same can happen with benchtop CNC milling machines, we might see more accelerated advancement that trickles down to more affordable machines.
Time will tell. In the meantime, I’ll start to save up, in case my optimism is well-placed.
